questions.question: Differentiate between KLL and LMM emission in AES. / Explain the mechanism of Internal Conversion and Intersystem Crossing
questions.solution_html:
• In Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES), transitions are named based on the three electron shells
  • involved. The first letter indicates the shell where the initial hole is created, the second indicates
  • the shell of the electron that fills the hole, and the third indicates the shell from which the Auger
  • electron is ejected. In KLL emission the incident beam creates a vacancy in the innermost K-shell
  • and the electron from the L-shell drops down to fill this vacancy. The energy released is then
  • transferred to a second electron in the L-shell, which is ejected. While in LMM emission the initial
  • vacancy is created in the L-shell. An electron from the M-shell falls to fill the L-shell hole, and the
  • resulting energy is used to eject another electron from the M-shell.

  • object dimensions are probed at the smaller recorded angles
  • SAXS is capable of delivering structural information for dimensions between 1 and 100 nm by
  • recording scattering at very small angles (0.1–10°)
  • Peak Area
  • The Core Principle: Field Emission
  • The heart of the FESEM is the Field Emission Gun (FEG).

questions.question: How Zeta potential depends on pH?
questions.solution_html:
• Zeta Potential is strongly influenced by the pH of the medium because pH affects the surface
  • charge of colloidal particles. As the pH changes, the concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺) and
  • hydroxide ions (OH⁻) around the particle surface also changes, altering the electrical double layer
  • and hence the zeta potential.
  • ● At low pH (acidic medium), the particle surface tends to adsorb more H⁺ ions, resulting in a
  • positive zeta potential.
  • ● At high pH (basic medium), adsorption of OH⁻ ions increases, producing a negative zeta
  • potential.
  • ● At a particular pH called the isoelectric point (IEP), the zeta potential becomes zero because the
  • positive and negative charges balance each other.
  • The magnitude of zeta potential determines the stability of colloidal systems. Higher positive or negative
  • zeta potential values indicate better colloidal stability due to stronger electrostatic repulsion between
  • particles.
  • (Definition:(1 marks); Explanation on effects: (3marks))
  • Analyzing biological materials.
questions.final_answer: Analyzing biological materials

questions.question: What is a Supporting electrolyte in Polarography?
questions.solution_html:
• A supporting electrolyte is an inert electrolyte added in large excess to the analyte solution to
  • increase its electrical conductivity and eliminate the migration current. It does not participate in the
  • electrode reaction but helps maintain a constant ionic strength throughout the experiment.
  • The supporting electrolyte ensures that the movement of electroactive species toward the electrode
  • occurs mainly by diffusion rather than by migration under the influence of an electric field. This
  • improves the accuracy and shape of the polarographic wave. Common examples of supporting
  • electrolytes include potassium chloride (KCl), potassium nitrate (KNO₃), and sodium sulfate
  • (Na₂SO₄).

questions.question: Explain the working of a SEM with the aid of a labelled diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• This technique provides high-resolution imaging and detailed information about the sample's surface
  • topography and composition. Scanning Electron Microscopy works on the principle of the interaction
  • between a focused beam of high-energy electrons and the surface of a specimen. In SEM, a beam of
  • electrons is generated by an electron gun and focused onto the sample surface using electromagnetic
  • lenses. When the electron beam strikes the specimen, various signals such as secondary electrons
  • backscattered electrons, and characteristic X-rays are produced due to electron–matter interactions.
  • The emitted secondary electrons are collected by a detector and converted into electrical signals to form a
  • highly magnified image of the sample surface. Since the electron beam scans the specimen point by point
  • detailed information about the surface morphology, texture, composition, and topography of the material
  • can be obtained.
  • Key Principles of SEM
  • a). Electron Beam Generation and Focusing, b). Scanning and Interaction c). Signal Detection and
  • Image Formation
  • (Working Principle-(4 marks), Labelled diagram -(3 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option . Electron Beam Generation and Focusing, b). Scanning and Interaction c). Signal Detection and

questions.question: Explain the working principle of AFM.
questions.solution_html:
• Atomic Force Microscope can analyze conducting as well as non-conducting materials and
  • provides detailed information about surface morphology, roughness, and nanoscale structures with
  • atomic-level resolution.
  • It works on the principle of measuring the force of interaction between a sharp probe tip and the surface
  • of a sample. In AFM, a very fine tip attached to a flexible cantilever scans across the surface of the
  • specimen. As the tip moves over the sample, attractive or repulsive forces between the atoms of the tip
  • and the sample cause the cantilever to bend or deflect.
  • A laser beam is focused onto the back of the cantilever, and the reflected beam falls on a photodetector.
  • The deflection of the cantilever changes the position of the reflected laser beam, which is converted into
  • electrical signals. These signals are processed by a computer to generate a high-resolution
  • three-dimensional image of the surface.
  • (Working Principle-(4 marks), Any schematic diagram -(3 marks))
questions.final_answer: (Working Principle-, Any schematic diagram -)

questions.question: Explain the basic principle of Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS). / Discuss the two primary mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement and mention two practical applications in nanotechnology.
questions.solution_html:
• mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement.
  • Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS): Amplifies signals by factors of 106 to 1011 using
  • localized electromagnetic fields on metallic nanostructures. SERS addresses the primary limitation
  • of standard Raman spectroscopy—its extremely low scattering cross-section.
  • Mechanisms involved in SERS
  • (a) Electromagnetic Mechanism (EM) is the dominant contributor to signal enhancement. It occurs
  • when the incident laser frequency matches the Localized Surface Plasmon Resonances (LSPR) of
  • noble metal nanostructures (like gold or silver). This creates a massive local electric field, and the
  • resulting Raman intensity scales approximately with the fourth power of this field enhancement.
  • (b) A secondary effect providing a smaller boost (factors of 101 to 103), which involves
  • charge-transfer processes between the metal surface and the adsorbed molecule, effectively acting
  • as a resonance Raman effect.
  • (c) Hot Spots: These are highly localized regions, such as the nanometric gaps between adjacent
  • particles or sharp metallic tips, where the electromagnetic field and signal enhancement are
  • exponentially higher than on flat surfaces.
  • (Definition: (3 marks); Mechanisms: Each explanation contains (2 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option Electromagnetic Mechanism (EM) is the dominant contributor to signal enhancement. It occurs

questions.question: / how is it useful for quantitative elemental analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• for quantitative elemental analysis.
  • X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), also known as Electron Spectroscopy for Chemical
  • Analysis (ESCA) is a widely used technique to investigate the chemical composition of the
  • surfaces.
  • Working Principle
  • XPS is based on the photoelectric effect. When a sample is bombarded with a beam of
  • monochromatic X-rays, the X-ray photons interact with the inner-shell electrons of the atoms in
  • the sample. Usually an Aluminum or Magnesium anode is used as the X-ray Source. If the energy
  • of the X-ray photon hv is greater than the binding energy (BE)of an electron, the electron is
  • ejected from the atom as a photoelectron. The kinetic energy of these emitted photoelectrons is
  • measured using an electron spectrometer.
  • The binding energy of the electron, which is characteristic of the element and its orbital, can be
  • calculated by Koopman's theorem.
  • KE = hv - BE - φ
  • Where:BE= Electron Binding Energy, KE= Electron Kinetic Energy,φ= Spectrometer Work
  • Function
  • Because each element has a unique set of binding energies, the resulting spectrum of intensity
  • versus binding energy allows for the identification of all elements (except hydrogen and helium)
  • present on the surface. The kinetic energy difference between the peak of the sample and
  • corresponding peak in a reference compound is known as chemical shift.The shifts of the
  • photoelectron lines in an ESCA spectrum reflect the increase in binding energy. ESCA chemical
  • shifts lie in the range 0-1500eV.
  • Quantitative Elemental Analysis
  • XPS is highly effective for quantitative analysis because the number of photoelectrons detected
  • for a specific element is directly proportional to its concentration within the sampled volume.To
  • determine the relative atomic concentration of an element, the following factors are used.
questions.final_answer: determine the relative atomic concentration of an element, the following factors are used

questions.question: Describe the basic intrumental features of FESEM with a schematic diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• The fundamental principle of FESEM (Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy) lies in its
  • unique method of generating electrons. While a standard SEM uses heat to "boil" electrons off a filament
  • FESEM uses a powerful electric field to pull them from a sharp needle-like tip. This results in a beam that
  • is much thinner, more coherent, and significantly higher in brightness, allowing for ultra-high-resolution
  • imaging down to 1 nanometer.
questions.final_answer: imaging down to 1 nanometer

questions.question: Explain the working of a SEM with the aid of a labelled diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• This technique provides high-resolution imaging and detailed information about the sample's surface
  • topography and composition. Scanning Electron Microscopy works on the principle of the interaction
  • between a focused beam of high-energy electrons and the surface of a specimen. In SEM, a beam of
  • electrons is generated by an electron gun and focused onto the sample surface using electromagnetic
  • lenses. When the electron beam strikes the specimen, various signals such as secondary electrons
  • backscattered electrons, and characteristic X-rays are produced due to electron–matter interactions.
  • The emitted secondary electrons are collected by a detector and converted into electrical signals to form a
  • highly magnified image of the sample surface. Since the electron beam scans the specimen point by point
  • detailed information about the surface morphology, texture, composition, and topography of the material
  • can be obtained.
  • Key Principles of SEM

  • Image Formation

questions.question: Explain the working principle of AFM.
questions.solution_html:
• Atomic Force Microscope can analyze conducting as well as non-conducting materials and
  • provides detailed information about surface morphology, roughness, and nanoscale structures with
  • atomic-level resolution.
  • It works on the principle of measuring the force of interaction between a sharp probe tip and the surface
  • of a sample. In AFM, a very fine tip attached to a flexible cantilever scans across the surface of the
  • specimen. As the tip moves over the sample, attractive or repulsive forces between the atoms of the tip
  • and the sample cause the cantilever to bend or deflect.
  • A laser beam is focused onto the back of the cantilever, and the reflected beam falls on a photodetector.
  • The deflection of the cantilever changes the position of the reflected laser beam, which is converted into
  • electrical signals. These signals are processed by a computer to generate a high-resolution
  • three-dimensional image of the surface.

questions.question: Explain the basic principle of Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS). / Discuss the two primary mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement and mention two practical applications in nanotechnology.
questions.solution_html:
• mechanisms responsible for the signal enhancement.
  • Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS): Amplifies signals by factors of 106 to 1011 using
  • localized electromagnetic fields on metallic nanostructures. SERS addresses the primary limitation
  • of standard Raman spectroscopy—its extremely low scattering cross-section.
  • Mechanisms involved in SERS
  • (a) Electromagnetic Mechanism (EM) is the dominant contributor to signal enhancement. It occurs
  • when the incident laser frequency matches the Localized Surface Plasmon Resonances (LSPR) of
  • noble metal nanostructures (like gold or silver). This creates a massive local electric field, and the
  • resulting Raman intensity scales approximately with the fourth power of this field enhancement.
  • (b) A secondary effect providing a smaller boost (factors of 101 to 103), which involves
  • charge-transfer processes between the metal surface and the adsorbed molecule, effectively acting
  • as a resonance Raman effect.
  • (c) Hot Spots: These are highly localized regions, such as the nanometric gaps between adjacent
  • particles or sharp metallic tips, where the electromagnetic field and signal enhancement are
  • exponentially higher than on flat surfaces.

questions.question: / how is it useful for quantitative elemental analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• for quantitative elemental analysis.
  • X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), also known as Electron Spectroscopy for Chemical
  • Analysis (ESCA) is a widely used technique to investigate the chemical composition of the
  • surfaces.
  • Working Principle
  • XPS is based on the photoelectric effect. When a sample is bombarded with a beam of
  • monochromatic X-rays, the X-ray photons interact with the inner-shell electrons of the atoms in
  • the sample. Usually an Aluminum or Magnesium anode is used as the X-ray Source. If the energy
  • of the X-ray photon hv is greater than the binding energy (BE)of an electron, the electron is
  • ejected from the atom as a photoelectron. The kinetic energy of these emitted photoelectrons is
  • measured using an electron spectrometer.
  • The binding energy of the electron, which is characteristic of the element and its orbital, can be
  • calculated by Koopman's theorem.
  • KE = hv - BE - φ
  • Where:BE= Electron Binding Energy, KE= Electron Kinetic Energy,φ= Spectrometer Work
  • Function
  • Because each element has a unique set of binding energies, the resulting spectrum of intensity
  • versus binding energy allows for the identification of all elements (except hydrogen and helium)
  • present on the surface. The kinetic energy difference between the peak of the sample and
  • corresponding peak in a reference compound is known as chemical shift.The shifts of the
  • photoelectron lines in an ESCA spectrum reflect the increase in binding energy. ESCA chemical
  • shifts lie in the range 0-1500eV.
  • Quantitative Elemental Analysis
  • XPS is highly effective for quantitative analysis because the number of photoelectrons detected
  • for a specific element is directly proportional to its concentration within the sampled volume.To
  • determine the relative atomic concentration of an element, the following factors are used.

questions.question: Describe the basic intrumental features of FESEM with a schematic diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• The fundamental principle of FESEM (Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy) lies in its
  • unique method of generating electrons. While a standard SEM uses heat to "boil" electrons off a filament
  • FESEM uses a powerful electric field to pull them from a sharp needle-like tip. This results in a beam that
  • is much thinner, more coherent, and significantly higher in brightness, allowing for ultra-high-resolution
  • imaging down to 1 nanometer.
